title: Meaningful motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps

concept.text: The innovation would reliably restore useful movement and protective sensation after a major peripheral nerve has been severed and a long segment is missing, including adult injuries repaired months later. A successful repair would allow regenerating nerve fibers to bridge the missing segment, reach appropriate muscles and sensory territories, and establish functional connections. The intended achievement is meaningful recovery across a difficult patient population; nerve fibers crossing a graft would be only an intermediate result.

Conceptual synthesis: this is a functional capability rather than a commitment to one graft material or treatment. Its proposed scope combines long gaps, delayed repair, and adult patients, conditions that make recovery particularly difficult. It concerns peripheral nerves supplying the limbs. Repair of the spinal cord and regeneration of an entire limb are separate capabilities.

significance.text: Major peripheral-nerve trauma can leave a mechanically intact limb with profound motor and sensory disability. Reliable recovery after delayed repair of long gaps would substantially expand reconstructive treatment for injuries with poor expected outcomes. The supplied review describes limitations serious enough that some patients are not offered repair surgery. The advance would therefore be greater reliability of functional recovery under adverse conditions, rather than simply the ability to attempt a long graft: the review already cites long-graft procedures.

Conditional clinical implications: appropriately targeted reinnervation could restore useful grip or gait and protective sensation after selected brachial plexus and extremity injuries, provided the relevant muscles and sensory targets remain receptive. These are plausible consequences of functional recovery, not outcomes demonstrated by the supplied evidence. Regeneration across the gap would not by itself establish coordinated movement, fine hand function, or recovery throughout a complex injury.

Limits on the impact: recovery after years of denervation, restoration of intrinsic hand muscles, and the cortical adaptation needed to use returning signals would require further evidence. Success in peripheral nerves would also not establish spinal cord regeneration, which involves a different central-nervous-system environment. The revolutionary claim is conditional on reliable functional target reinnervation within the tested injury population.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is timely functional reinnervation across long adult nerve gaps despite delayed treatment. The supplied review describes a race between axon growth and declining biological support. Regeneration takes time, while aging and prolonged axotomy—the period during which a neuron remains disconnected from its target—can reduce neurons' capacity to extend axons. In long grafts, Schwann cells can lose their repair-supporting phenotype before regenerating axons reach the distal region. These mechanisms draw partly on experimental models and should not be treated as uniform behavior in every clinical injury.

Engineering synthesis: a successful treatment would have to sustain neuronal growth and a supportive environment throughout the bridge, then deliver enough functional connections to the intended distal targets before those targets become unreceptive. The required performance is simultaneous motor and sensory recovery, so anatomical continuity or a count of crossing axons would leave the central clinical question unanswered.

Targeting remains an additional concern. Persistent axonal misrouting after some fibers reconnect was asserted in the earlier candidate, but the supplied review does not establish that specific claim. It remains a proposed barrier requiring separate evidence. Functional testing should nevertheless distinguish useful target reinnervation from connections that fail to produce the intended movement or sensation.

For platelet-rich plasma, or PRP, approaches specifically, reproducible preparation and application are unresolved engineering issues. The review describes variable efficacy and an absence of standardized techniques. Promising recovery reports therefore leave open which preparation, delivery method, and repair conditions could produce consistent benefit across patients.

current_state.text: In their mini review published on 27 May 2025, Foy and Kuffler report that fewer than 50% of patients recover meaningful function even under relatively favorable conditions. Their introduction characterizes favorable prognosis as restricted to repair within about five months, gaps under 5 cm, and patients no older than approximately 20–25 years. It also summarizes particularly poor recovery when two or all three factors—delay, gap length, and age—become less favorable together. These numbers describe the authors' synthesis of cited literature, not a newly measured population estimate or a prediction for every patient.

The review states that few axons regenerate across grafts at least 8 cm long and that no axons cross autografts longer than 10 cm. These statements should remain attributed to that review rather than become universal biological cutoffs. The underlying studies were not supplied for independent assessment, and the review's references include long-graft procedures. Poor reliability therefore does not establish that surgeons never attempt these repairs or that all longer grafts are categorically incapable of supporting regeneration.

The review describes promising clinical recovery reports involving PRP-containing repairs, including a case report under difficult repair conditions. It also emphasizes variable efficacy and the lack of standardized PRP preparation and application. These reports provide preliminary clinical observations, but they do not establish the proposed controlled, population-level endpoint of joint motor and sensory recovery after delayed repair of long adult gaps. The supplied evidence does not justify characterizing all these reports as small clinical series or establishing PRP as a standard treatment for this population.

Evidence boundary: the supplied review assessment describes complete retained HTML and PDF copies containing the article body, conclusion, and references, with no recorded extraction problems. They are two copies of one review, not independent corroboration. The supplied material does not establish approved nerve-conduit indications, and the empty freshness record does not establish the field's status as of 1 November 2026. These limitations constrain the conclusions available here; they do not show that the dated recovery reports are false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration, not an established clinical standard: enroll adults older than 25 with a mixed motor-sensory nerve gap longer than 8 cm, repaired more than six months after injury. By three years after repair, most enrolled patients should achieve both Medical Research Council grade 4 or better in preregistered target muscles and protective sensation in a preregistered skin territory. Grade 4 denotes movement against resistance. The joint endpoint should be assessed at the patient level so that motor recovery in one group and sensory recovery in another cannot be combined into an apparent success.
completion_criteria.label: Most patients achieve MRC≥4 and protective sensation by three years

completion_criteria.text: Proposed trial requirements: compare the treatment with an appropriate autograft or allograft control and preregister the required comparative result. Specify the sensory test and threshold, the target muscles and rules for combining their results, the numerical meaning of success in most patients, sample size, and handling of missing outcomes. Including a control alone would not define whether the intended result is superiority or another clinically justified comparison. Outcome assessment should be sufficiently independent and consistent to make the functional comparison credible.
completion_criteria.label: Controlled functional comparison meets preregistered success and assessment criteria

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: require a sufficiently sized controlled study and independent replication using a reproducible treatment protocol. Report safety, durability through the three-year endpoint, rehabilitation requirements, and outcomes by nerve, gap length, delay, age, and target condition. If PRP is used, specify its preparation and application so another team can reproduce the intervention. Isolated case reports would not meet this proposed bar, and successful finite trials would establish demonstrated breadth within their populations rather than universal effectiveness across peripheral-nerve injuries.
completion_criteria.label: Independent controlled replication with reproducible protocol and reported practical boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ORT-01, Adult epimorphic regeneration of a functional limb, would need functional nerve integration as part of a much broader reconstruction. ORT-07 addresses one enabling capability within that challenge; it does not regenerate the limb's other tissues or establish their coordinated development. ORT-06, Force-bearing skeletal muscle after volumetric muscle loss, is closely complementary: muscle restoration concerns rebuilding force-producing tissue, while ORT-07 concerns reconnecting neural input and sensory pathways. Neither capability alone guarantees that the other has been solved.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-04, Regeneration of the load-bearing tendon–bone enthesis, and ORT-10, Single-episode restoration of segmental long bone by vascularized, remodelable bone, address structural components that may also be damaged in severe extremity trauma. They could complement nerve recovery in a reconstructed limb, but restoring an attachment or bone segment does not establish neural function, and restoring a nerve does not repair those load-bearing structures.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-02, Biological restoration of the osteoarthritic synovial joint, and ORT-05, Restoration of the intervertebral disc as a living load-bearing organ, share a goal of biological restoration of musculoskeletal function. Their principal targets are joints and discs, respectively, rather than a missing peripheral-nerve segment. ORT-05 also should not be conflated with spinal cord regeneration or with the peripheral-nerve capability described here.

Roster-based synthesis: ORT-03, Eradication of mature biofilm in bone and on orthopedic implants without removing the reconstruction, could help preserve a reconstruction complicated by infection, but it addresses microbial eradication rather than nerve regeneration. ORT-08, Anatomically precise and reversible control of osteogenesis, concerns control of bone formation, and ORT-09, Regeneration of a functioning growth plate, concerns restoration of longitudinal skeletal growth. Their overlap with ORT-07 is at the level of orthopedic reconstruction and biological control; each remains a distinct innovation.

change_log.change: Preserved ORT-07's identity and defined success as reliable joint motor and sensory recovery after delayed long-gap adult repair.
change_log.reason: The useful innovation is functional recovery in a difficult population; axon crossing alone does not establish that capability.

change_log.change: Integrated the neuronal and Schwann-cell mechanisms while qualifying their clinical generality.
change_log.reason: The review supports these mechanisms, partly through experimental models, without establishing identical behavior in every patient.

change_log.change: Retained persistent misrouting as an explicitly unverified proposed concern.
change_log.reason: The supplied review does not substantiate persistence after reconnection, but that evidence gap does not justify discarding the innovation.

change_log.change: Preserved the 2025 numerical claims with explicit attribution and limits on interpretation.
change_log.reason: The recovery percentage, age, delay, and distance statements are review summaries; the underlying studies were not supplied for independent assessment.

change_log.change: Replaced the suggestion that long gaps exceed autograft practice with a claim about poor reliability of recovery.
change_log.reason: The review itself cites long-graft procedures, so poor prognosis cannot establish absence of surgical practice.

change_log.change: Recast PRP evidence as preliminary clinical reports, including a case report, and added variability and standardization barriers.
change_log.reason: The supplied assessment does not establish the blanket description of small clinical series or the proposed controlled population-level result.

change_log.change: Removed the categorical assertion about approved conduit gap indications and bounded the current-state account by its evidence date.
change_log.reason: Regulatory indications and developments through 1 November 2026 are not established by the supplied material.

change_log.change: Made grip, gait, prolonged-denervation recovery, and cortical adaptation explicit conditional implications or remaining challenges.
change_log.reason: They are useful clinical distinctions but are not demonstrated outcomes in the supplied review.

change_log.change: Refined the proposed completion endpoint, comparison, reproducibility requirements, and limits of generalization.
change_log.reason: The review recommended grade 4 or better, a joint patient-level endpoint, predefined sensory testing and comparative results, and explicit handling of missing outcomes.

change_log.change: Explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry without combining their identities.
change_log.reason: Nerve recovery can enable broader reconstruction while remaining distinct from muscle, bone, joint, growth-plate, infection, and whole-limb capabilities.

unresolved_issues: The supplied freshness record is empty; developments after the May 2025 review and the field's status on 1 November 2026 remain unestablished.

The underlying studies supporting the review's recovery percentage and age, delay, and graft-length statements were not supplied for independent assessment; their applicability across nerves and injury patterns remains unresolved.
Persistent axonal misrouting after partial reconnection requires evidence beyond the supplied review.
The effectiveness and reproducibility of particular PRP preparations and application methods in delayed long-gap adult repairs remain unresolved.
Approved conduit indications and their relevance to this population are not established by the supplied material.
The proposed trial still requires a numerical patient-level success threshold, sensory test, muscle aggregation rule, sample size, missing-data plan, and required comparative effect.
Recovery after years of denervation, restoration of intrinsic hand muscles, cortical adaptation, and generalization across complex brachial plexus injuries remain separate questions.

brief.title: Restoring movement and feeling after severe nerve injuries
possible: After a severe limb injury, people could regain useful movement and feeling that warns them of harm, even when a long section of nerve is missing and surgery happens months later.
why: A limb can remain physically intact yet lose movement and sensation because its nerves are severed. Reliable repair could restore useful grip or walking and expand treatment for people whose injuries currently have poor prospects.

sources.who: Christian A. Foy and Damien P. Kuffler
sources.showed: Their review describes poor functional recovery after nerve repair, especially as gaps, treatment delays and patient age increase. It also discusses preliminary reports of recovery with experimental repairs.
sources.quote: even under relatively good conditions, <50% of patients recover meaningful function.
sources.cited_for: The review explains why reliable recovery across long gaps after delayed repair remains difficult.
sources.not_established: A review of preliminary reports does not establish consistent recovery of both movement and protective sensation in this population.

sources.who: Christian A. Foy, William F. Micheo and Damien P. Kuffler
sources.showed: A single older patient regained normal sensation after delayed repair of long nerve gaps. Nerve fibers reached the intended muscles, but muscle contractions remained minimal.
sources.quote: Evoked contractions were minimal due to poor muscle fiber recruitment.
sources.cited_for: The case demonstrates sensory recovery and some muscle reconnection under difficult repair conditions.
sources.not_established: A single case with minimal contractions does not demonstrate useful strength or reliable recovery across patients.

sources.who: Blair R. Peters, Matthew D. Wood, Daniel A. Hunter and Susan E. Mackinnon
sources.showed: In a selected series of failed repairs using donor nerve tissue stripped of cells, patients had no clinical movement or sensory recovery. Nerve fibers failed to enter or progress through the transplanted tissue.
sources.quote: Histology demonstrated myelinated axons present in all proximal native nerve specimens.
sources.cited_for: These failures illustrate barriers to restoring function through transplanted nerve tissue.
sources.not_established: A series selected for failed repairs cannot establish how often this treatment fails overall.

shown: Foy and colleagues have reported substantial sensory recovery alongside limited muscle reconnection in a single difficult case. Reliable return of useful strength and protective sensation together across adults with long gaps and delayed treatment remains undemonstrated.
missing: A treatment must keep nerve fibers growing across the whole gap before the disconnected muscles and sensory targets lose their ability to recover.
Most treated patients must regain both useful strength and protective sensation, rather than merely have nerve fibers cross the gap.
Independent controlled studies must establish repeatable benefits, safety and the limits of recovery across patients and injuries.

milestones.label: Most patients regain strength and protective sensation
milestones.explanation: Most eligible adults with long gaps repaired after a prolonged delay would have to regain movement against resistance and protective sensation within 3 years. Recovery must include both abilities in the same patients.

milestones.label: A controlled trial meets success rules set in advance
milestones.explanation: A trial would have to meet predefined success rules through independent, consistent testing against repair using the patient's or a donor's nerve tissue. This would establish the treatment's comparative benefit.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce recovery and establish practical limits
milestones.explanation: An independent team would have to repeat a sufficiently large controlled study with a reproducible protocol, reporting safety, lasting recovery, rehabilitation and patient and injury limits. This would establish reliability.

uncertain: The patient-level success threshold, sensory test, muscle scoring rules and required comparative benefit still need definition.
It remains unclear which experimental repair preparations and delivery methods could produce consistent benefits.
Recovery after years without nerve input, fine hand function and outcomes across complex injuries remain open questions.

page.title: Motor and sensory recovery across long peripheral-nerve gaps
page.definition: Adults recover movement and sensation after repair of mixed limb nerves across gaps longer than 5 cm, including injuries repaired more than 90 days after trauma. Mixed nerves contain both motor fibres, which activate muscles, and sensory fibres, which carry signals from the tissues.

goal.need: Foy and Kuffler’s review, published on 27 May 2025, reports meaningful functional recovery in fewer than 50% of patients even under relatively favourable conditions. RANGER registry results show incomplete recovery after longer-gap repairs and differences between limbs. Its motor or sensory recovery rates do not establish simultaneous recovery of both functions after chronic injury.

figures.caption: RANGER registry outcomes for 50–70 mm nerve-gap repairs, published in 2020
figures.note: Industry-sponsored observational data. Meaningful recovery denotes the applicable motor or sensory threshold, not a patient-level joint endpoint; these are not exclusively chronic repairs.

statements.body: US Department of Defense, Tissue Injury and Regenerative Medicine Project Management Office
statements.quote: Areas of intended DOD investment in this area focus on products that can speed nerve regrowth.
Current treatment options, such as autografts, have limitations, so this approval addresses a significant unmet medical need for patients with peripheral nerve injuries.
statements.context: FDA announcement of Avance approval on 3 December 2025.

completion.title: A controlled study establishes joint recovery after chronic long-gap nerve repair.
completion.criterion: A prospectively registered controlled study in adults aged ≥18 years with mixed limb-nerve gaps >5 cm repaired >90 days after injury meets its prespecified superiority criterion against nerve autograft for the patient-level proportion achieving both MRCC motor grade ≥M3 and sensory grade ≥S3 at 24 months. The same patients must meet both thresholds. This joint comparative test is an Atlas proposal; no numerical majority requirement is imposed.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas proposal, combining published clinical scope definitions and recovery thresholds; no outside body was found to have published this combined test.
completion.basis: Searches covered FDA approval documents, registered nerve-repair protocols, NICE guidance, society guidelines and DoD programmes. No published test combined adult age, chronic repair, long gaps and patient-level joint recovery. The proposal uses published MRCC recovery thresholds, the RANGER chronic-injury category, the >5 cm clinical scope and FDA’s 24-month assessment interval. Superiority addresses improvement over autograft without inventing a required recovery percentage.

milestones.title: A 5-cm nerve-gap repair restores distal muscle responses in a large animal at 12 months.
milestones.criterion: In the published porcine common-peroneal-nerve model, a repaired 5-cm segmental defect supports axons distal to the graft and evoked compound muscle action potentials in downstream muscles at 12 months. Smith and colleagues demonstrated these outcomes with tissue-engineered grafts and autografts; Figure 8 reports 3 animals per group at that time point. This establishes target reinnervation, not voluntary motor or sensory recovery in people.
milestones.set_by: Smith and colleagues, published porcine study protocol and Figure 8, 2022; this is an experimental benchmark, not a human gap-length equivalence.
milestones.threshold_quote: Axon regeneration and functional reinnervation at 12 months following repair of 5-cm CPN segmental defects in swine.

milestones.title: Human muscle becomes reinnervated across a long repaired nerve gap.
milestones.criterion: Needle electromyography detects reinnervating motor units in a target muscle beyond a repaired nerve gap. On 22 September 2021, Foy and colleagues reported muscle reinnervation across a 9-cm gap in one 56-year-old man repaired 2.6 years after trauma; evoked contractions remained minimal, despite S4 sensory recovery across two 11-cm gaps. Peters and colleagues’ selected series of 5 failed median or ulnar allograft repairs had no clinical or electrophysiological recovery, showing that proximal axons alone do not establish this milestone.
milestones.set_by: Clinical electrodiagnostic convention, described by Bateman and colleagues in their postoperative assessment guidance.
milestones.threshold_quote: Needle EMG is an effective post‐operative tool to assess for reinnervation of recipient muscles, demonstrated by nascent units

milestones.title: Human nerve-gap repairs reach motor grade ≥M3 or sensory grade ≥S3.
milestones.criterion: The applicable MRCC threshold is ≥M3 for motor recovery—movement against gravity—or ≥S3 for sensory recovery—pain and touch sensation without over-response. A report published on 26 October 2026 described 8 men aged 18–58 years with 10 upper-limb mixed-nerve repairs: gaps 2–12 cm, repair delays 0.1–3.25 years and follow-up 10 months–17.8 years. Four repairs reached ≥M3 and 7 reached ≥S3. The uncontrolled, unblinded series did not establish a joint responder rate for chronic gaps >5 cm.
milestones.set_by: Meaningful-recovery convention used in the RANGER registry and subsequent clinical studies; these are separate functional thresholds, not a joint population success standard.
milestones.threshold_quote: Meaningful recovery was defined to be S3 or M3 or greater to remain consistent with previously published results.

milestones.title: A randomized study verifies motor and sensory clinical benefit at 24 months after mixed-nerve repair.
milestones.criterion: FDA requires a prospective, randomized, assessor-blinded, multicentre comparison of Avance with sural nerve autograft in adults aged ≥18 years with mixed or motor nerve gaps >25 mm. Clinical benefit must be verified using MRCC motor and sensory recovery at Month 24, with sensory assessment applying to mixed repairs. FDA’s assessment dated 3 December 2025 stated that definitive clinical benefit remained unestablished. This requirement does not specify a chronic-repair minimum or a joint responder rate for gaps >5 cm.
milestones.set_by: US Food and Drug Administration, Avance approval letter dated 3 December 2025, required confirmatory study ANG-CP-013; published for Avance and gaps >25 mm.
milestones.threshold_quote: increased motor strength and improvement of sensation measured by Medical Research Council Classification (MRCC) motor and sensory at Month 24.

not_found: No outside completion test combining adult chronic long-gap repair with patient-level joint motor and sensory recovery was found.
No published joint recovery rate restricted to adults with both gaps >5 cm and repair delays >90 days was found.
The accessible FDA documents do not provide the numerical comparative success margin for ANG-CP-013.
Full ClinicalTrials.gov records for NCT05541250 and NCT07657182 and NICE’s recommendation page could not be retrieved.
The PMC full text of Peters and colleagues’ failure series was inaccessible; its publisher’s abstract was accessible.

results.finding: One patient had muscle reinnervation across a 9-cm ulnar nerve gap.
results.detail: Repair occurred 2.6 years after injury. Electromyography detected reinnervation, but evoked contractions were minimal.
results.quote: Electromyography studies established motor axon reinnervation of adductor digiti minimi and first dorsal interosseous muscle fibers.

results.finding: One patient achieved S4 sensory recovery across two 11-cm nerve gaps.
results.detail: The sensory branches were repaired 2.6 years after injury. The report does not establish motor recovery of M3 or greater.
results.quote: The sensory recovery by both sensory nerve branches was S4.

results.finding: Five patients with median or ulnar nerve allograft repairs had no motor unit response on electromyography.
results.detail: The selected series had no clinical or electrophysiological evidence of recovery; proximal axons did not establish target-muscle reinnervation.
results.quote: Electromyography revealed evidence of muscle denervation but no motor unit response.

results.finding: Five patients with failed median or ulnar nerve allograft repairs had no clinical sensory or motor recovery.
results.detail: Patients were selected because their repairs had failed; the series does not demonstrate recovery to the MRCC thresholds.
results.quote: All patients included in this series had no clinical sensory or motor recovery and had significant neuropathic pain ranging from 8 to 10/10 on a visual analogue scale.

results.finding: Pigs with 5-cm common-peroneal nerve repairs had distal axons and evoked muscle responses at 12 months; n=3 per group.
results.detail: Tissue-engineered grafts and autografts supported distal axon regeneration and muscle responses. These findings demonstrate reinnervation in pigs, not voluntary motor or sensory recovery in people.
results.quote: For all repair strategies assessed, the histological findings were corroborated via positive electrophysiological recordings at 9 and 12 months (

results.finding: One 19-year-old man had motor unit potentials detected after repair of a 15-cm common peroneal nerve defect.
results.detail: Before surgery, needle EMG showed no motor unit response during maximum voluntary contraction. Six months after grafting, motor unit potentials were recorded in the peroneal brevis.
results.quote:
Six months postoperatively, Tinel’s sign extended to the distal site, and MUP of the peroneal brevis was 
recorded using needle electromyography.

results.finding: Of 2 sciatic nerve repair patients, 1 regained MRC grade 5/5 motor function in the tibial distribution.
results.detail: The patient’s graft was approximately 7.5 cm long. Time from injury to repair was not reported; peroneal dorsiflexion reached MRC grade 2/5.
results.quote: In the postoperative period the patient regained motor function (Medical Research Council [MRC] Grade 5/5) in the tibial distribution, with partial function in peroneal distribution (MRC Grade 2/5 on dorsiflexion).

results.finding: One adult with a lower-limb tibial nerve repair reached MRC grade 4 in toe flexors.
results.detail: The initial nerve defect was 15 cm, and coaptation occurred about six months after injury. The report gives an MRC grade for toe flexor muscles, but does not explicitly report an MRCC motor grade for the nerve repair.
results.quote: After 8 years of follow‐up, the patient achieved an MRC grade of 4 for toe flexor muscles and attained protective sensibility in the right plantar region.

results.finding: Among 11 lower-limb mixed-nerve repairs spanning 50–70 mm, 36% reached ≥S3 or ≥M3.
results.detail: The 50–70 mm category includes gaps exactly 5 cm long. The reported subgroup results do not establish recovery in repairs that were both longer than 5 cm and performed more than 90 days after injury.

results.finding: In pigs with mixed-nerve repairs, 3 TENG-treated animals had evoked muscle responses after 5-cm gaps.
results.detail: The study reported evoked muscle responses and compound muscle action potentials in pigs. It did not report needle EMG evidence of reinnervating motor units in humans, and the repaired gaps were 5 cm.
results.quote: Nerve stimulation proximal and distal to the repair site elicited robust muscle movement, and positive hoof eversion was observed, corroborating the CMAP recordings.

results.finding: One patient achieved tibialis anterior manual muscle test grade 3 at 2 years.
results.detail: A 15-cm common peroneal nerve defect was repaired with a sural nerve graft. The report uses manual muscle testing and does not identify the grade as MRCC.
results.quote: Furthermore, 2 years postoperatively, MMT of TA improved to grade 3, and the patient could walk without a knee brace.

results.finding: One patient regained tibial motor function after repair with an approximately 7.5-cm graft.
results.detail: The report describes clinical motor recovery but does not report needle electromyography detecting reinnervating motor units.
results.quote: The graft length was approximately 7.5 cm. In the postoperative period the patient regained motor function (Medical Research Council [MRC] Grade 5/5) in the tibial distribution, with partial function in peroneal distribution (MRC Grade 2/5 on dorsiflexion).

results.finding: One adult recovered toe-flexor strength to MRC grade 4 after repair of a 15-cm tibial nerve defect.
results.detail: The clinical motor recovery is consistent with reinnervation, but the report does not describe needle electromyography detecting reinnervating motor units.
results.quote: After 8 years of follow‐up, the patient achieved an MRC grade of 4 for toe flexor muscles and attained protective sensibility in the right plantar region.

results.finding: One adult had motor and sensory recovery 8 years after treatment of a 15-cm tibial nerve defect.
results.detail: This uncontrolled case used nerve lengthening and end-to-end suturing. It did not compare Avance with autograft, assess benefit at 24 months, or report an MRCC sensory grade.
results.quote: After 8 years of follow‐up, the patient achieved an MRC grade of 4 for toe flexor muscles and attained protective sensibility in the right plantar region.

results.finding: Of 52 upper-extremity repairs assessed for motor function, 69% achieved at least M3.
results.detail: Clinical motor recovery is indirect evidence of reinnervation. The study does not report needle EMG findings or establish the gap lengths for this subgroup.

results.finding: Of 6 lower-extremity repairs assessed for motor function, 17% achieved at least M3.
results.detail: Clinical motor recovery is indirect evidence of reinnervation. The study does not report needle EMG findings or establish the gap lengths for this subgroup.

results.finding: Of 61 upper-extremity mixed-nerve repairs, 79% achieved at least S3 or M3.
results.detail: This observational registry used variable follow-up and historical comparisons; it was not the randomized, assessor-blinded autograft comparison at 24 months required by the criterion.

results.finding: Of 16 lower-extremity mixed-nerve repairs, 44% achieved at least S3 or M3.
results.detail: This observational registry used variable follow-up and historical comparisons; it was not the randomized, assessor-blinded autograft comparison at 24 months required by the criterion.

results.finding: Lower-limb nerve reconstruction in 12 patients: early common peroneal repairs reached muscle strength grade ≥4.
results.detail: The report does not identify the grading scale as MRCC or state how many patients were in the early-repair subgroup. It reports inadequate muscle function in late cases.
results.quote: For common peroneal nerve reconstructions, all patients with denervation time less than 6 months regained muscle strength of grade at least 4, even when long grafts were used for defects of 20 cm or more.

results.finding: Single 26-year-old man with a 14-cm median-nerve gap had ENMG evidence of thenar reinnervation at 1 year.
results.quote: ENMG performed 1 year after surgery revealed significant reinnervation of the thenar eminence, and the final follow-up assessment displayed complete reinnervation of the hand and median nerve.

results.finding: Single 26-year-old man with a 14-cm median-nerve gap reached M5 and S3+ at final follow-up.
results.quote: Our assessment demonstrated skin tropism and sufficient muscle power to act against strong resistance (M5) in the muscles previously affected by paralysis, as well as a good localization of stimuli in the median nerve region and an imperfect recovery of two-point discrimination (S3+).

results.finding: Single 26-year-old man with a 14-cm median-nerve gap reached M4/S3+ at 24 months.
results.detail: Single uncontrolled case report; not randomized, assessor-blinded, or multicentre, and no comparison with autograft.
